name: Privacy, copyright and your online identity
intro: Your digital footprint and online identity, how to protect your own and others' privacy, and how to use other people's work fairly with copyright, Creative Commons and source lists.
sammendrag:
## Your digital footprint

Everything you do online leaves a **digital footprint**: posts, comments, likes, pictures, searches and the apps you use. Some of it is **active** (what you post yourself) and some is **passive** (data collected about you, like your location). Your footprint can be seen by friends, schools and future employers – and by companies that use your data for advertising.

## Privacy

**Privacy** is your right to control information about yourself. **Personal data** is any information that can identify you: your name, address, phone number, photos and even your IP address. In Norway and the rest of the EEA, the **GDPR** gives you rights, such as the right to see what data a company has about you and the right to have it deleted.

Tips to protect your privacy:

- Use strong, different **passwords** and **two-step verification**.
- Check your **privacy settings**.
- Think before sharing your location or personal details.
- Never share your passwords, not even with friends.

## Respecting others

You are also responsible for **other people's privacy**. Always ask for **consent** before posting pictures or videos of others. Sharing embarrassing or private content can hurt people – and may be illegal.

## How do you present yourself online?

The way you present yourself online is your **online identity**. Many people show only the best sides of their lives – edited photos and highlights. Ask yourself: Is this how I want to be seen? Would I be OK with this post in five years? Remember that other people's online lives are often just as edited as yours.

## Copyright

**Copyright** protects the people who create **original works**: texts, photos, music, films, drawings and games. In Norway, copyright lasts until 70 years after the creator's death. This means you cannot freely use other people's work in your own projects.

- **Quote** short parts and always **credit** the source.
- Use pictures and music with a **Creative Commons** licence or from free image libraries, and follow the licence terms.
- Or create your own pictures and music!

## Using sources honestly

Using someone else's words or ideas without saying where they come from is called **plagiarism**. It is dishonest, and in school it can be treated as cheating. Always include a **source list** with the author, title, website and date you read it.

flashcards.def: What you post yourself, like pictures, comments and likes.
Data collected about you without you noticing, like your location.
Your right to control information about yourself.
Information that can identify you, like your name, photo or IP address.
EU privacy rules that also apply in Norway.
Settings that decide who can see what you share.
An extra security step, like a code sent to your phone.
A clear yes to something, like having your picture shared.
The way you present yourself online.
The creator's right to decide how their work is used. Lasts until 70 years after death.
Licences that let creators allow others to use their work on certain conditions.
Saying who made something and where it comes from.
Using someone else's words or ideas without saying where they come from.
A list of the sources you have used, with author, title, website and date.

options: The details stored in your account
The traces you leave online
The messages sent to your inbox
The settings saved on your device
quiz.explain: Posts, likes and searches all become part of your footprint.

quiz.text: Which of these is personal data?
options: A public weather forecast
A common cooking recipe
Your phone number
A famous painting
quiz.explain: Personal data can be linked to you as a person.

quiz.text: What does the GDPR give you the right to?
options: Have a website remove a post you dislike
Get compensation for every data leak
Choose which pictures others post online
Have your personal data deleted
quiz.explain: This is often called “the right to be forgotten”.

quiz.text: What should you do before posting a picture of a friend?
options: Ask for their consent
Check whether the photo looks flattering
Tag them after you post it
Choose a filter that suits the picture
quiz.explain: Everyone has the right to decide over pictures of themselves.

quiz.text: How long does copyright last in Norway?
options: Until 50 years after the creator's death
Until 70 years after the work is published
Until 100 years after the creator's death
Until 70 years after the creator's death
quiz.explain: After that, the work becomes free for everyone to use.

options: Using a spell checker to fix your writing
Using others' words or ideas without naming the source
Writing a long text in your own words
Quoting someone and naming the source
quiz.explain: Plagiarism is a form of cheating.

quiz.text: What is a Creative Commons licence?
options: A licence that transfers ownership to every user
A label that means the work has no copyright
A licence letting others use work under certain conditions
A rule that prevents people from sharing a work
quiz.explain: For example, you may have to credit the creator.

quiz.text: Why should you think before posting?
options: Your digital footprint may remain visible to others for years
Websites charge a fee for each post you make
Posts disappear from other people's phones when deleted
Posts use more mobile data than videos do
quiz.explain: Future schools and employers may see what you post.

quiz.text: Which is a good way to protect your privacy?
options: Use one memorable password for all your accounts
Use strong, different passwords and two-step verification
Save your password in a public profile
Share your login details with trusted friends
quiz.explain: Strong passwords make it harder for others to access your accounts.

quiz.text: What is a passive digital footprint?
options: Information you choose to share, like a profile photo
A comment you write and publish on a website
A like you give to another person's post
Data collected about you, like your location
quiz.explain: Passive data is collected in the background.

ekstra.text: An IP address can be personal data.
ekstra.explain: It can be used to link online activity to you.

ekstra.text: If a picture is on the internet, you can use it freely.
ekstra.explain: Pictures online are still protected by copyright.

ekstra.text: You should include a source list when you use sources.
ekstra.explain: It shows where your information comes from.

ekstra.text: Most people show a completely realistic picture of their lives online.
ekstra.explain: Many people share mostly edited highlights.

ekstra.text: What does it mean to credit a source?
options: To pay the creator for using their work
To say who made it and where it comes from
To remove the creator's name from a work
To copy a work into your own project
ekstra.explain: Crediting is fair to the creator and honest to the reader.

ekstra.text: Which of these is protected by copyright?
options: A song someone wrote
A music style such as pop
A singer's birthday date
A fact about a famous musician
The password you use to enter a website
The account balance shown by your bank
The way you present yourself online
The home address written on your mail
ekstra.explain: Your posts, profile and comments build your online identity.

skriv.text: Compare an active digital footprint with a passive digital footprint. Give one example of each.
skriv.fasit: An active footprint is something you post yourself, such as a comment. A passive footprint is data collected about you, such as your location.
kriterier: Explains that an active footprint comes from things you do or post yourself.
Explains that a passive footprint is data collected about you, and gives a suitable example.

skriv.text: How can the things you do online affect how other people see you in the future? Include who may see your digital footprint.
skriv.fasit: Friends, schools and future employers may see your digital footprint. What you post or do online can affect the impression they get of you.
kriterier: Names at least one relevant audience, such as schools or future employers.
Connects the digital footprint to the impression those people may get.

skriv.text: Sam wants only friends to see a photo he shares online. What should he check or change, and how would that help?
skriv.fasit: Sam should check his privacy settings and choose who can see the photo. These settings decide who can see what he shares.
kriterier: Says to check or change the privacy settings.
Explains that the settings control who can see the photo or other shared content.

skriv.text: Explain how two-step verification adds an extra security step when someone signs in.
skriv.fasit: After entering a password, the person must complete another step, such as entering a code sent to their phone. This makes signing in require more than just the password.
kriterier: Explains that a second step is needed in addition to the password.
Gives a suitable example, such as a code sent to a phone.

skriv.text: You use information from a website in a school assignment. What details should you put in your source list?
skriv.fasit: Include the author, the title, the website and the date you read it.
kriterier: Includes the website and the date the source was read.

skriv.text: A classmate’s online profile shows edited photos and highlights. Explain why this may not show the whole of their life.
skriv.fasit: Many people show only the best sides of their lives online, using edited photos and highlights. Other people’s online lives may be edited too.
kriterier: Explains that people may choose to show only the best sides of their lives.
Mentions that photos or other parts of an online profile may be edited.

skriv.text: You want to use someone else’s photo in a project. Give two ways to do this while respecting copyright.
skriv.fasit: You could use a photo with a Creative Commons licence and follow its terms, or choose one from a free image library and follow the licence terms. You could also make your own photo.
kriterier: Suggests using a Creative Commons photo or one from a free image library.
Says to follow the licence terms, or suggests creating an original photo instead.

skriv.text: Explain the difference between copyright and plagiarism.
skriv.fasit: Copyright is the creator’s right to decide how their original work is used. Plagiarism is using someone else’s words or ideas without saying where they came from.
kriterier: Explains that copyright concerns the creator’s control over how their work is used.
Explains that plagiarism is using another person’s words or ideas without naming the source.
